lessons.title: Yield, Appreciation and Total Return Compared

children.text: Two siblings in Bengaluru each inherit ₹1.5 crore. Priya buys a 3BHK on Sarjapur Road and rents it out. Rahul buys a pre-leased office unit on the Outer Ring Road. At every family dinner for the next ten years they argue. Priya points to how much her flat has appreciated. Rahul points to the rent landing in his account every month. Both are measuring half the picture. This lesson puts residential and commercial property on the same scale, total return, using one consistent 10-year model so you can see which really wins, and under what conditions.

body.text: Commercial property pays most of its return in cash along the way. Residential property saves most of its return for the day you sell. Judge both on total return, never on yield or appreciation alone.

body.latex: \text{Total Return} = \text{Income Return (net rent)} + \text{Capital Return (change in value)}
body.caption: Both parts must be measured after costs: stamp duty on entry, running costs and vacancy during the hold, and brokerage on exit.

markDefs.definition: The annual return that makes the present value of all cash flows from an investment, including the purchase, yearly income and final sale, equal to zero. It rewards cash received earlier.
Total cash received from an investment, including income and sale proceeds, divided by the total cash invested. It ignores timing.

The Model: Same Money, Same 10 Years

body.caption: Assumptions for ₹1.5 crore invested without a loan

cells: 3% owner costs plus 10% vacancy and re-leasing allowance
Price grows at 4%, 6% or 8% a year
Year 11 rent divided by exit cap rate of 7.25%, 8.25% or 9.25%

children.text: The commercial exit cap rates bracket the entry level of about 8.25% (the in-place rent after owner costs, divided by price). An exit at 8.25% means the market values the office the same way at sale as at purchase. At 9.25%, buyers see a 10-year-older building as riskier. At 7.25%, the market has become more optimistic.

stats.label: Flat price growth needed to match
Net rent collected: office vs flat

children.text: Under these assumptions, even the office's weaker scenario beats the flat's strongest one. For the flat to match the office's neutral case, its price would need to grow at about 9.5% a year for a full decade, a pace few micro-markets sustain. Note also that the office's value only grows about 4.2% a year in the neutral case. It wins through rent, not appreciation.

body.title: Flat, 6% growth: sources of total gain
Office, neutral exit: sources of total gain

children.text: The flat earns about 71% of its gain from the sale price, which you receive only at the end and only if the market cooperates. The office earns about 67% of its gain as rent you collect along the way. Cash in hand earlier is worth more, which is why IRR favours the office by more than the money multiples alone suggest.

columns.label: Residential
points: Outcome driven by local price growth
Lower volatility of rent, higher reliance on the market at sale
Wins only if appreciation is strong and sustained

columns.label: Commercial
points: Return spread across the holding period
Outcome driven by tenant, lease and exit cap rate
Lumpy rent if a tenant leaves
Wins if occupancy holds and cap rates do not rise sharply

body.text: This model flatters commercial property if its assumptions fail. A 10% vacancy allowance may be too low for an ageing strata building, where one bad re-leasing cycle can cost 16 months of rent. And a 2 percentage point jump in exit cap rate would cut the office's sale value sharply. The office wins on paper. It wins in practice only with a sound tenant, a good building and realistic exit assumptions.

In commercial property, the exit cap rate is the most important assumption nobody talks about. In this model, each 1 percentage point change in the exit cap rate moves the 10-year IRR by roughly 1 percentage point. Always ask what cap rate a buyer will pay in ten years, for a building ten years older.

body.title: How the model handles timing and simplifications

children.text: Cash flows are annual. Year 0 is the purchase including stamp duty. Years 1 to 10 are net rent. Year 10 also includes net sale proceeds. IRR is the rate at which these cash flows net to zero.
The office's exit value uses year 11 rent after owner costs, ₹18.81 lakh, divided by the exit cap rate, less 1% brokerage. Its rent steps up 15% at the start of years 4, 7 and 10.

The model ignores loans, income tax and capital gains tax, which Chapter 4 covers separately, and assumes both properties are held without major capital spending. Real outcomes will differ, but consistent assumptions make the comparison fair.

body.title: Estimate: A Quick Total Return
body.prompt: A pre-leased shop in Jaipur has a net yield of 7.5%, and you expect its value to grow about 3% a year. Using the simple rule total return ≈ income return + capital return, what is its approximate annual total return, in %?
body.explanation: 7.5% + 3% = 10.5%. This quick estimate ignores entry and exit costs and the timing of cash flows, which usually pull the real IRR slightly lower.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: Why IRR
body.textWithBlank: Unlike the money multiple, IRR accounts for the ___ of cash flows, so rent received earlier counts for more.
body.explanation: Two investments can return the same money multiple, but the one that pays cash earlier earns a higher IRR, because that cash can be used or reinvested sooner.

body.title: Quick Check: The Biggest Swing Factor
body.question: In the office model, which single assumption changes the 10-year IRR most between the scenarios shown?
body.explanation: Moving the exit cap rate from 7.25% to 9.25% changes the office's IRR from 11.4% to 9.6%. Stamp duty and brokerage were identical across scenarios, and the flat's rent growth does not affect the office.

body.title: Scenario: Settling the Sibling Argument
body.scenario: Ten years on, Priya's Sarjapur Road flat has grown in value at 7% a year. Rahul's Outer Ring Road office had one tenant change in year 6, which left it empty for 10 months. The building now looks dated next to newer campuses, and brokers suggest buyers would want a 9.5% cap rate. Each claims to have won.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's model as a guide, who probably did better, and what should each of them take away?
body.modelAnswer: It is likely close. Priya's 7% growth sits between the model's 6% and 8% flat scenarios, suggesting an IRR of about 8%. Rahul's office would have scored about 10.5% in the neutral case, but he suffered two setbacks the model only partly allowed for: a 10-month vacancy, likely worse than the 10% annual allowance once rent-free months and brokerage are added, and an exit cap rate of 9.5%, worse even than the model's weakest 9.25% scenario, which delivered 9.6%. Together these could pull his IRR down towards Priya's. Priya's lesson: she won on appreciation, which was never guaranteed, and her rent contributed little. Rahul's lesson: commercial property's advantage depends on occupancy and building quality, and an ageing building erodes it through both vacancy and a higher exit cap rate. Both should compare using total return after costs, not their favourite half of the picture.

cards.definition: Income return plus capital return, measured after all costs.
Net rent as a percentage of the amount invested.
The change in property value, net of transaction costs, over the holding period.
The annual return that accounts for the size and timing of all cash flows.
Total cash received divided by cash invested; ignores timing.
The cap rate a buyer applies when you sell; a key driver of commercial returns.

points: Compare property on total return after costs: net rent plus change in value, including stamp duty and brokerage.
In a consistent 10-year model, a flat returned about 5.5% to 9.1% a year depending on price growth, while a pre-leased office returned about 9.6% to 11.4% depending on exit cap rate.
The flat needed about 9.5% annual price growth for a decade to match the office's neutral case.
Residential return is mostly capital gain received at exit; commercial return is mostly rent received along the way.
IRR rewards earlier cash, so commercial property's rent-heavy profile scores better than money multiples alone suggest.
Commercial advantage depends on occupancy, building quality and the exit cap rate, and can shrink quickly if these go wrong.

body.text: The model uses simplified, illustrative assumptions and excludes loans and taxes. It is not a forecast of returns for any property, city or segment. Actual outcomes depend on specific assets, markets and costs. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy any property.
